content:
Urban Indians aren't capitalists. They're feudal in their logic.

Capitalism, at its core, demands optimisation. 

Price, productivity, efficiency, quality and long term returns. But much of urban India's consumer behaviour doesn't operate on those principles. It operates through status, imitation, hierarchy and social validation.

Take the iPhone.

A capitalist consumer should compare price, performance, durability and total cost of ownership. But many people don't make the decision that way. They buy an iPhone because it is popular, heavily marketed and socially validated.

A ₹40,000 phone may provide most of the functionality at a fraction of the cost, but the iPhone carries status. It signals income, success and belonging to a particular social class.

The same logic applies to cars.

People often don't buy the most efficient car for their actual needs. They buy the car that signals success. An SUV becomes desirable not simply because of its utility, but because of what owning that SUV communicates socially.

This is why I call it feudal logic rather than capitalist logic.

The question isn't simply:
"What gives me the highest value for my money?"

It becomes:
"What does the dominant class consider valuable?"

The individual then imitates the dominant class and seeks validation from the people around them.

This is where M. N. Srinivas's concept of Sanskritization becomes useful. Social mobility often occurs through the imitation of the practices, lifestyles and consumption patterns of groups perceived as socially superior.

Urban consumer culture can reproduce a similar mechanism.

People don't merely consume products. 
They consume symbols of status.
The iPhone and the SUV are therefore not just economic goods. 
They can become instruments of social positioning.

What looks like individual choice can actually be class imitation operating through the marketplace.

The market provides the products.

The hierarchy provides the preferences.
